\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

Serving multimodal RAG at scale is a GPU provisioning problem with two levers: routing reduces generation compute
per query relative to always combining both contexts, and index placement handles visual-index memory as the corpus grows. Measured end to
end with real retrieval and generation on one GPU, the strongest fixed policy is the page image alone. The
content-aware router CAVR-CE gains 0.016 ANLS over it for 15\% more GPU compute, and uses 29\%
less GPU compute than always combining text and image contexts at a mean ANLS cost of 0.008. On 1,499
held-out questions from the training splits, which the generator may have seen, the frozen router kept a
35\% saving over always-hybrid, but its gain over the page image alone ($+0.005$ ANLS, interval
[-0.004, +0.014]) was not significant: whether routing beats the best single path depends on whether the OCR text
helps on a given question distribution, and on our held-out set the comparison may also reflect training exposure. In a load test simulated from measured service times, 100 queries/s at
p95 $\le$ 2\,s needs 72 GPUs with CAVR-CE, 106 with always-hybrid and
64 with always-visual. Served live with vLLM on one and two A10 GPUs, the policies kept this
order and CAVR-CE sustained 1.82$\times$ the arrival rate of always-hybrid at p95 $\le$ 5\,s,
but absolute capacity at that target was 1.4--2.0$\times$ lower than simulated, and at
2\,s one A10 missed the target with CAVR-CE and always-hybrid even at the lowest tested rate, so the simulated GPU
counts are estimates whose error at larger pools is unknown. Its cost weight is a per-deployment setting; confidence-based
escalation reached the same operating point as lowering it.

On two multi-GPU nodes (three Tesla P40 and two NVIDIA A10 GPUs), sharding the visual index
holds exhaustive search at constant latency as the corpus grows with the number of GPUs, with parallel efficiency
of at least 99.6\% and 97.6\% from 50k pages up. With the index in host memory,
two GPUs searched a million pages in large batches at close to the throughput per GPU of GPU-resident search,
which would need 16 GPUs; the price is single-query latency (6.4\,s), which limits this
placement to batch search.

The evaluation also shows what does not hold. The gain over the best fixed path did not carry over to new
questions, the keyword rule behind our earlier labels does not reflect which path answers correctly, and with a
shared generator the text path is not a cheap path. A per-query oracle (ANLS 0.630 at 0.486 GPU-s) shows how much remains: the
bottleneck is predicting, before generation, whether a path will succeed.

The routing results come from one GPU, the serving results from a simulation checked live on two GPUs for generation
only, and sharding and the host-memory index were measured on
separate server nodes for retrieval only. Future work should serve retrieval, routing and generation together on a larger cluster, model the interference
of prefills with running requests in the capacity simulator, find an overload signal that lets $\lambda$ follow load, improve per-query success
prediction, and extend routing to queries that contain images.
